sinks.name: Object.assign
sinks.severity_note: P4 as a client-side prototype pollution primitive; upgrades to P2/P3 only when a concrete gadget (polluted property consumed by a sanitizer bypass or innerHTML) is demonstrated.
sinks.explain: Object.assign(target, source) copies enumerable own properties from source to target using [[Set]] semantics. When source comes from JSON.parse(attackerData), an own property literally named '__proto__' exists (JSON.parse does NOT trigger the setter), and assigning it to target invokes the inherited __proto__ setter — silently retargeting the object's prototype or writing onto Object.prototype when target is a shared object.
sinks.how_it_works: Two ingredients make Object.assign dangerous: (1) JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"x":1}}') produces an object with a genuine own '__proto__' key — the parser does not special-case it; (2) Object.assign's internal Set(target, '__proto__', value) DOES trigger Object.prototype's __proto__ setter. If the pattern is Object.assign(sharedConfig, JSON.parse(tainted)), the attacker's object becomes sharedConfig's prototype, and every property lookup on sharedConfig falls through to attacker-controlled values.
sinks.why_it_matters: Prototype pollution is a confusion primitive: it adds or overrides properties on objects the attacker never touches directly. Client-side, its impact is gated by gadgets — polluted properties like 'innerHTML', 'src', or sanitizer allowlists that later code trusts — but when a gadget exists the result is full DOM XSS from a pure data payload.

steps.action: Confirm a tainted JSON string reaches Object.assign as a source
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?cfg={"__proto__":{"jlf":"polluted"}}' then run ({}).jlf or inspect the merge target's prototype in the console
steps.indicator: the merge target's [[Prototype]] now exposes jlf:'polluted', or ({}).jlf === 'polluted' if Object.prototype itself was hit

steps.action: Pollute a property the application later trusts
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?cfg={"__proto__":{"innerHTML":""}}' in a browser
steps.indicator: code that copies an object's properties onto a DOM node (a common gadget) assigns the polluted innerHTML and alert(document.domain) fires

chains.eligibility: Client-side prototype pollution is accepted when paired with a working gadget leading to XSS or security-control bypass; pollution with no observable gadget impact is usually rated informational/low — always hunt the gadget before reporting.

steps.action: Pollute via an attacker-influenced API response that gets merged
steps.indicator: the PUT is accepted and a subsequent GET of https://TARGET/api/prefs returns the __proto__ key verbatim

steps.action: Load the page that merges the stored response and check for pollution
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page' in a browser, wait for the fetch+merge, then run ({}).jlf in the DevTools console
steps.indicator: ({}).jlf === 'polluted' confirms Object.prototype pollution sourced from a stored server value

chains.eligibility: Server-stored pollution payload + client-side merge = stored client-side PP; accepted at the severity of whatever gadget it arms.

contexts.html-body: Pollution itself renders nothing; the gadget decides the context. A polluted 'innerHTML' property lands in html-body context.
contexts.attr: Polluted properties like 'src' or 'href' arm attribute gadgets (e.g. script src from a polluted default).
contexts.js-string: Polluted configuration values consumed by eval-like templating arm js-string gadgets.

sinks.waf_notes: The payload is valid JSON and often travels in the URL fragment or a JSON body — both poorly inspected by WAFs. '__proto__' as a string rarely matches XSS signatures.
sinks.eligibility: Be honest: client-side PP usually needs a gadget to matter. Report P4/informational for pollution alone; P2/P3 only with a demonstrated gadget chain to script execution or sanitizer bypass.
mitigations: Reject or strip '__proto__', 'prototype', and 'constructor' keys before merging untrusted objects
Use Object.create(null) for merge targets and dictionaries
Freeze Object.prototype in security-critical contexts (Object.freeze(Object.prototype)) as a last-resort hardening
Prefer structuredClone or explicit field whitelisting over blanket Object.assign of parsed JSON
references: OWASP: Prototype Pollution Prevention Cheat Sheet

sinks.name: _.merge (lodash)
sinks.severity_note: P4 client-side; P2/P3 with a gadget. Historical CVEs (CVE-2018-3721, CVE-2019-10744, CVE-2020-8203) — check the lodash version; unpatched versions are vulnerable by default.
sinks.explain: _.merge(destination, source) deep-recursively copies source properties into destination. When source is attacker JSON containing a '__proto__' key, lodash's recursive merge walks INTO the prototype chain and assigns properties onto Object.prototype — classic client-side prototype pollution (also _.defaultsDeep and _.set with tainted paths).
sinks.how_it_works: Unlike Object.assign, _.merge recurses: for key '__proto__' it resolves destination['__proto__'] (the actual Object.prototype via the accessor) and then merges the attacker's nested object into it, e.g. _.merge({}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"x":1}}')) sets Object.prototype.x = 1 in vulnerable versions. Every object in the page now inherits the polluted property. _.set(obj, taintedPath, value) is the path-based twin: _.set({}, '__proto__.x', 1) pollutes directly.
sinks.why_it_matters: lodash is everywhere — bundlers inline it into most large apps. A single _.merge of user-controlled JSON gives the attacker a global, persistent-for-the-session write into every object's property resolution, which is exactly what DOM XSS gadgets (sanitizer config, attribute defaults, template options) consume.

steps.action: Fingerprint lodash and the vulnerable merge of tainted JSON
steps.indicator: a merge/defaultsDeep/set call whose source or path derives from location, postMessage, or an API response

steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#config={"__proto__":{"jlf":"polluted"}}' then run ({}).jlf in the console
steps.indicator: ({}).jlf === 'polluted' — Object.prototype was polluted through the merge

steps.action: Arm a gadget with the pollution
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#config={"__proto__":{"innerHTML":""}}' in a browser
steps.indicator: the gadget code (property-copy-to-DOM, template render, or sanitizer default) consumes the polluted property and alert(document.domain) fires

chains.eligibility: Accepted with a gadget; also report the outdated lodash version itself (known CVE) — many programs pay for the dependency finding even before the gadget chain is complete.

steps.action: Deliver a pollution payload through the message listener
steps.command: open a page that posts this JSON string to the target's message listener, then read {}.jlf in the victim console
steps.indicator: {}.jlf === 'polluted' in the victim page — prototype is polluted

steps.action: Escalate via a gadget reachable in the same page
steps.payload: pollute a property a later sink trusts (e.g. {"__proto__":{"innerHTML":""}})
steps.command: target the specific property the page's sink reads
steps.indicator: the gadget path turns pollution into script execution

chains.eligibility: Accepted as High when you demonstrate a gadget (pollution -> XSS or logic bypass). Pollution without a demonstrated gadget is usually rated Low-Medium.

contexts.html-body: Gadget-dependent: polluted innerHTML/html/template options land in html-body context.
contexts.attr: Polluted attribute defaults (src, href, style) arm attribute gadgets.
contexts.js-string: Polluted config strings consumed by new Function/eval-based templating arm js-string gadgets.

sinks.waf_notes: Payloads are JSON with '__proto__' keys — syntactically benign and typically delivered via fragment or POST body where WAF inspection is weakest.
sinks.eligibility: Same honest rule: gadget or it is informational. The exception is a known-vulnerable lodash version, which is independently reportable as a vulnerable-dependency finding.
mitigations: Upgrade lodash to the latest 4.x (PP fixes landed across 4.17.12-4.17.21) and pin it
Replace _.merge of untrusted data with explicit whitelisted field copies
Sanitize keys ('__proto__', 'constructor', 'prototype') before any deep merge or path set

sinks.name: $.extend (jQuery deep)
sinks.severity_note: P4 client-side; P2/P3 with a gadget. CVE-2019-11358: jQuery < 3.4.0 deep-extends '__proto__' into Object.prototype — extremely widespread in legacy apps.
sinks.explain: $.extend(true, target, source) is jQuery's deep recursive extend. In versions before 3.4.0, when source (attacker JSON) contains a '__proto__' key, the deep copy writes the nested properties onto Object.prototype. Even in >= 3.4.0 the '__proto__' key is skipped, so the vulnerable versions are the target — and they are still common in legacy admin panels and CMS plugins.
sinks.how_it_works: The vulnerable code path: $.extend(true, {}, JSON.parse(tainted)) iterates keys; for '__proto__' it takes target['__proto__'] — the real Object.prototype through the accessor — and recursively copies the attacker's nested object into it. One call pollutes every object in the page. jQuery's ubiquity in older stacks makes this the single most common client-side PP source in the wild.
sinks.why_it_matters: Any legacy page that deep-extends URL/postMessage/API JSON with jQuery < 3.4.0 is one payload away from session-wide Object.prototype pollution; combined with the rich jQuery plugin ecosystem (which reads options objects everywhere), gadgets are rarely far away.

steps.action: Check the jQuery version and find the deep extend of tainted data
steps.command: grep -n 'extend(true' app.js; grep -n 'jquery' app.js | grep -i '1\.\|2\.\|3\.[0-3]' | head
steps.indicator: jQuery < 3.4.0 is loaded AND a $.extend(true, target, taintedJSON) call exists

steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?opts={"__proto__":{"jlf":"polluted"}}' then run ({}).jlf in the console
steps.indicator: ({}).jlf === 'polluted' confirms Object.prototype pollution via the deep extend

steps.action: Arm a gadget through plugin options or a DOM property copy
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?opts={"__proto__":{"innerHTML":""}}' in a browser
steps.indicator: a plugin or template that copies options onto DOM nodes assigns the polluted innerHTML and alert(document.domain) fires

chains.eligibility: Report both layers: the vulnerable jQuery version (dependency finding, accepted widely) and, if a gadget exists, the full PP-to-XSS chain at XSS severity. Pollution without a gadget is informational.

steps.action: Identify an API response merged deep into page state
steps.command: grep -n 'extend(true' app.js and trace which fetch/XHR feeds the second argument
steps.indicator: a JSON API response flows into a deep extend — server-reflected or tampered data can pollute

steps.action: Pollute via the response (or a MITM/compromised API)
steps.command: if the API reflects any user input, send the payload there; verify {}.jlf in the page console
steps.indicator: {}.jlf appears — the extend path pollutes the prototype from remote data

chains.eligibility: Valid when the polluted data source is attacker-influenceable (reflected API input, compromised feed). Purely static API data lowers it to Informational.

contexts.html-body: Gadget-dependent; plugin option objects copied to innerHTML land in html-body context.
contexts.attr: Polluted href/src defaults arm attribute gadgets in jQuery plugins.
contexts.js-string: Polluted template strings arm js-string gadgets in jQuery templating plugins.

sinks.waf_notes: JSON '__proto__' payloads via query string or POST body; the fragment variant bypasses server inspection entirely.
sinks.eligibility: Be precise about the version: on jQuery >= 3.4.0 this specific vector is dead ('__proto__' is skipped) — do not report it as exploitable there; look for $.extend of already-polluted objects instead.
mitigations: Upgrade jQuery to >= 3.4.0 (fixes CVE-2019-11358) and prefer the latest 3.x
Never deep-extend untrusted JSON; copy only whitelisted fields

sinks.name: dynamic path assignment obj[a][b]=v
sinks.severity_note: P4 client-side; P2/P3 with a gadget. This is the raw hand-rolled variant — no library required — so it hides in bespoke config-merge and form-serialization code.
sinks.explain: Hand-written deep-set logic like obj[parts[0]][parts[1]] = value — where the path parts come from the attacker (JSON keys, form field names like 'a[b]', URL params) — walks straight into '__proto__': obj['__proto__']['x'] = 1 writes onto Object.prototype. No lodash or jQuery needed; the language itself is the vulnerability.
sinks.how_it_works: Property access with the string '__proto__' resolves through the accessor to the object's prototype. So a loop that does current = current[part] for part in path, then current[lastKey] = value, traverses obj['__proto__'] into Object.prototype when the attacker supplies it, and the final assignment pollutes every object. Classic carriers: query-string parsers that expand 'a[b][c]=v' into nested objects, and form serializers that do the same with input names.
sinks.why_it_matters: Because it is dependency-free, static analysis rules tuned for _.merge/$.extend miss it. Any custom 'parse the query string into an object' helper is a candidate, and those helpers exist in almost every large front-end codebase.

steps.action: Find the bracket-notation deep-set or query parser that builds nested objects
steps.indicator: a loop or helper that assigns into nested keys derived from URL parameters or form field names

steps.action: Traverse into Object.prototype with a __proto__ path
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?__proto__[jlf]=polluted' then run ({}).jlf in the console
steps.indicator: ({}).jlf === 'polluted' — the parser walked __proto__ and polluted Object.prototype

steps.action: Arm a gadget via the polluted property
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?__proto__[innerHTML]=' in a browser
steps.indicator: the gadget consumes the polluted property and alert(document.domain) fires

chains.eligibility: Same honest bar as all client-side PP: with a demonstrated gadget it is accepted at gadget severity (XSS = P2/P3); bare pollution is informational. The hand-rolled parser itself is the root cause — report it precisely.

steps.action: Find deep-set built from form input names
steps.command: inspect form fields for dotted/bracketed names; submit with __proto__-style keys (name="__proto__.jlf")
steps.indicator: the page's parser builds obj['__proto__']['jlf'] — check {}.jlf in console

steps.action: Confirm pollution and hunt the gadget
steps.command: submit the form, then trigger the page path that reads the polluted property
steps.indicator: polluted property is consumed by a sink — execution or logic change

chains.eligibility: Form-driven pollution is accepted when a gadget is shown. Note honestly in the report if no gadget was found — usually Medium.

contexts.html-body: Gadget-dependent: polluted html/innerHTML properties land in html-body context.
contexts.attr: Polluted src/href defaults arm attribute gadgets.
contexts.js-string: Polluted strings consumed by eval-style templating arm js-string gadgets.

sinks.waf_notes: Bracket-notation parameters (?__proto__[x]=y) look like ordinary form encoding; very few WAF rules inspect parameter NAMES for '__proto__', and the fragment variant never reaches the server.
sinks.eligibility: Gadget-gated like all client-side PP. Note for triage: demonstrate ({}).pollutedKey in the console as the minimal proof, then the gadget detonation for severity.
mitigations: In any deep-set helper, refuse keys '__proto__', 'prototype', and 'constructor' before traversal
Build parsed objects with Object.create(null) so no prototype accessor exists to traverse
Use a vetted query-string library with pollution protection instead of hand-rolled parsing
Validate form field names against a schema before serializing into objects
references: OWASP: Prototype Pollution Prevention Cheat Sheet
